You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failing test `testListAllFilesWithNestedArchive` attempts to iterate over a ZIP file's entries and also tries to create nested `ArchiveInputStream` instances from each entry. It expects exactly one `ZipException` to be thrown for entries that are not valid nested ZIP files.

The current bug report points out that the `getNextEntry` method (mapped to `getNextZipEntry()` in `ZipArchiveInputStream`) incorrectly returns `null` when encountering an invalid ZIP entry. This behavior makes it impossible to differentiate between two distinct conditions:
- The end of the archive (no more entries),
- An invalid entry that could not be parsed properly.

Looking at the code for `ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry`:
- It reads the next local file header (LFH).
- If the LFH signature is a central file header or an archive end signature, it marks the end of entries, skips the remaining archive, and this eventually leads to returning `null`.
- If the signature is not a valid local file header signature, it returns null.
- The method catches EOFException on reading and returns null, which signals no more entries.
- However, returning null is also the fallback when the signature read is not a local file header signature (line 248-249).

This means that if the stream encounters some invalid entry or data (potentially not a ZIP entry or damaged), the method returns null instead of throwing an exception. This causes the calling code (the test case) to be unable to recognize that an invalid entry was encountered. The test expects an exception (a ZipException) when reading a non-ZIP entry as a nested archive, but `getNextZipEntry()` does not throw or propagate this exception for invalid entries.

Hence, the bug is that `getNextZipEntry` conflates "end of archive" (which should return null) with "invalid entry encountered" (which should throw an exception). The test's logic to detect expected exceptions fails because the method returns null prematurely when there is an invalid entry.

The recent bug reports do not explicitly mention this particular behavior, though one mentions subtle handling of junk bytes at the end of entries, which may conceptually relate to how signatures or entries are validated.

Conclusion:
`getNextZipEntry()` must be modified to throw an exception (likely `ZipException`) when an invalid entry (non-local file header signature, corrupted data, etc.) is encountered instead of silently returning null. This will allow callers to differentiate between "no more entries" and "invalid entry found".

Such a change aligns with the user's current bug report and the failing test case's expectations of exception handling when nested archives are invalid.

This diagnosis explains why the test `testListAllFilesWithNestedArchive` fails: it expects to catch a `ZipException` but this is not thrown due to the current implementation returning null on invalid entries, leading to test assertion failure on the count of expected exceptions.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
